action_summary: Runs the previous round's pre-registered falsifier and answers it: a record-based commit DOES recover byte-exactly from a crash between two single-path renames, so multi-path commits have a sound portable implementation and last round's residual -- atomic only where the filesystem can exchange two populated paths -- is dissolved rather than engineered around. A 6-operation real commit (GNU tar extracting five members, rm deleting one) is crashed at all 10 boundaries: before the record the tree is provably still the pre-state and there is no record (all-or-nothing); at and after the durable record all 8 boundaries recover to the target byte-exactly; a crash after cleanup finds the target with nothing to replay. Recovery is itself crashed inside every one of its steps: 56 of 56 second recoveries reach the target. The no-record control leaves a tree that is neither state at 5 of 9 boundaries with nothing to recover from -- exactly why the previous round's single-rename limit was real. 868-byte record, 16 fsyncs, 7 renames per 6-operation commit. The durable record, not the sequence of renames, is the commit point.
